tagline: Patrick Henry’s last political speech and final home in Virginia’s hilly Charlotte County
intro: Route 40 passes through Charlotte Court House and continues west through Phenix toward Brookneal. Charlotte County is predominantly rural and hilly; its southwestern boundary is the Roanoke River, locally called the Staunton. Near Drakes Branch, Charlotte State Forest lies off Saxkey Road, a Virginia Scenic Byway.

Red Hill’s location on the Staunton River served the plantation’s transportation needs. Patrick Henry bought Red Hill in 1794 and lived there until his death in 1799. That March, he gave his last political speech at Charlotte Courthouse, opposing the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.

Randolph lies near the Staunton River and is home to Staunton River Battlefield State Park. At Charlotte Court House, Route 40 meets Route 47 in the town center. Westward, Phenix is six miles from Charlotte Court House; Red Hill lies near Brookneal, with Henry’s grave and reconstructed home.

moments.title: Randolph
moments.text: A railroad supply line made the Staunton River bridge a target in June 1864. Union cavalry sought to cut the railroads supplying Confederate forces at Petersburg. Captain Benjamin L. Farinholt ordered a train to run repeatedly to a station farther south, creating the impression that reinforcements kept arriving. The defenders held the bridge, preserving the supply line. Part of the battlefield is preserved in the state park; Randolph’s Roanoke visitor center occupies a railroad depot and holds exhibits on Native Americans and railroad history. The park straddles the river in Halifax and Charlotte counties.

moments.title: Charlotte Court House
moments.text: Charlotte Court House marks the end of Patrick Henry’s public political speaking. In March 1799, he spoke here against the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions. The settlement’s name changed repeatedly: incorporated as The Magazine in 1756, it became Daltonsburgh in 1759, then Marysville in 1836 and Smithville in 1874. Charlotte Courthouse followed in 1901, with the present name adopted in 1989. Many buildings in the central courthouse area date from the 1800s. Routes 40 and 47 cross in the center of town. Charlotte Court House is also the county seat, near the center of Charlotte County.

moments.title: Red Hill
moments.text: The house at Red Hill is a reconstruction of Patrick Henry’s last home. He bought the plantation in 1794 and lived here with Dorothea and their children until his death in 1799. This was a working tobacco plantation with quarters for enslaved people, located on the Staunton River for transportation. In the 1950s and 1960s, the Patrick Henry Memorial Foundation restored his law office and preserved his grave. In 2018, it acquired the Quarter Place, which housed enslaved and later free Black populations at Red Hill. The Quarter Place contains a cemetery holding the remains of 147 enslaved people.
